As we are moving forward with Doctronics, we are defining what the included capabilities are. Requirements to be defined.

*Initial description:* Provides safe, clear guidance on prescription and over-the-counter medications and supplements, including usage, side effects, interactions, coverage context, and neutral comparisons where appropriate. People often ask whether a medication is safe to take, what to watch for, or how it fits into their overall care.

*User & moment*
_Who is this for? What situation are they in when they ask this?_
• Has a prescription or OTC medication question
• Wants to understand side effects, interactions, or contraindications
• Trying to understand coverage (e.g., ODB) or get a rough sense of cost
• Wants reassurance or clarification about a medication they’re taking or were prescribed
• Experiencing a symptom and wondering if it could be medication-related
*User goal (in their words)*
_“I want to know ___ so I can ___.”_
• “I want to know how to take this safely so I can avoid side effects.”
• “I want to know if this medication could be causing my symptoms so I know what to do next.”
• “I want to know if this is covered so I can plan my purchase.”
• “I want to know what risks to watch for so I’m not caught off guard.”
*System job*
_What must the system help them decide or do?_
• Clarify which medication(s) the question applies to
• Explain safe use, common side effects, and meaningful risks in plain language
• Incorporate relevant context when available (other meds, known conditions, age)
• Help the user decide whether to monitor, adjust behaviour, or seek professional help
• Set clear boundaries around what requires a pharmacist or clinician
*Happy path (MVP)*
_Step-by-step, plain language. No UI details. No components._
1. User asks a medication-related question
2. System clarifies the medication and the nature of the concern
3. System provides clear, grounded guidance with citations where relevant
4. Systems informs about coverage under insurance
5. System explains common vs concerning effects or interactions
6. System offers a clear next step (monitor, talk to a pharmacist, seek care)
*Decision point*
_What choice or action should the user be confident in by the end?_
• “I understand how to take this safely.”
• “I know whether this symptom could be related to my medication.”
• “I know if I should talk to a pharmacist or clinician next.”
• “I understand whether coverage applies and what that means for me.”
*Trust requirements*
_What would make this feel unsafe, confusing, or untrustworthy?_
• Contradictory or inconsistent answers across similar questions
• Information that feels incomplete or overly vague
• Language that is alarmist or, conversely, dismissive of risk
• Lack of clarity around what the system can and cannot advise
• Coverage information that is outdated or inaccurate
*Explicit non-goals (MVP)*
_What are we not doing yet?_
• Diagnosing conditions based on symptoms
• Changing doses or prescribing medications
• Managing complex polypharmacy
• Completing medication purchases or refills in chat
• Replacing pharmacist or clinician judgment
• Providing precise or personalized cost estimates
• not altering details or language of response based on medication risk tiering (i.e. be more cautious while responding about riskier meds)

Design the first-time Remedy experience that sets clear expectations, builds trust, and explains safety boundaries before meaningful interaction begins.

*Context*
Users will arrive with assumptions shaped by ChatGPT and Google. If we do not explicitly frame Remedy’s role, we risk either overselling or confusing users.

*What needs to be designed*
 Design the first-time experience that explains:
• What Remedy can help with
• What it cannot do
• When it will escalate to human support
• How safety is handled: This should feel calm, clear, and confidence-building, not legalistic.
*Output*
 End-to-end first-time user flow and draft copy patterns.

*Description*
AI-generated responses may include phone numbers, URLs, email addresses, and physical addresses.
These should remain inline within the conversational text wherever possible, with clear, lightweight CTAs that allow users to take action (call, open link, email, open maps) without breaking conversational flow.
This is about enabling action while preserving a natural chat experience.

*Design requirements / cases to consider*
Inline-first vs elevation
• Entities remain embedded in text by default.
• Define when (if ever) an entity should be elevated beyond inline treatment.
Clear action affordances
• Phone → tap to call
• URL → handled to be gracefully displayed → tap to open
• Email → tap to compose
• Address → map?
Visual consistency
• Actionable entities are visually distinct from regular text.
• Avoid clutter when multiple entities appear in one response.
Emergency handling
• Emergency numbers visually differentiated from standard numbers.
Accessibility
• Adequate tap targets on mobile.

Remedy currently exists as a mobile-only experience within the iOS apps. We need to design and deliver a web version that maintains the core Remedy experience while adapting to desktop/browser contexts and interaction patterns.
The web experience should feel native to browser environments while preserving the conversational flow, personalization features, and core functionality that users expect from Remedy. This expansion will increase accessibility and reach for users who prefer desktop interactions for health guidance.

*Design Requirements / Cases to Consider*
• Responsive design across desktop, tablet, and mobile web viewports
• Web-specific interaction patterns (hover states, keyboard navigation, right-click contexts)
• Browser compatibility and progressive enhancement
• URL structure and deep linking capabilities
• Integration with existing web properties (PC Health web, Shoppers web)
• Session management and login state across web platforms
• Accessibility compliance for web standards (WCAG)
• Performance considerations for web chat interfaces
• Mobile web vs. native app experience differentiation

• Android-specific interaction patterns (navigation gestures, hardware back button)

Users often need to share visual information with healthcare providers: photos of symptoms, medication bottles, test results, or documents. Remedy currently only supports text-based conversations, limiting users' ability to get comprehensive guidance on visual health concerns.

We need to design a file upload experience that allows users to share images and relevant documents with Remedy while maintaining appropriate privacy, security, and medical guidance boundaries. This will enable more comprehensive health conversations and better support for visual health questions.

*Design Requirements / Cases to Consider*
• Chat UI: how uploads fit within chat interface
• Image capture vs. gallery selection vs. document upload flows
• File preview and confirmation before sending to Remedy
• Remedy's capability to analyze and respond to visual content appropriately
• Error handling for unsupported files, upload failures, etc
• Loading states and processing time communication for file analysis
